##### **Introduction** 

###### **What will be the key drivers in 2011?** 

Base metals finished 2010 on a firm note with exceptional gains seen in December, ranging from 9.6% for aluminium to as high as 17.1% for lead.  GFMS’ Base Metals Index, which gives equal weight to all the base metals unlike the LME index that is heavily skewed towards aluminium and copper, gained 14.2% during December.  The index started the year at 292.75, troughed at 231.84 on June 8 and then ended the year on a high

of 363.4.  The extreme nature of the rally in 2010 left the index only just below the all-time high achieved in the previous bull market of 394.98.  On January 6 2011, the GFMS Base Metal index stood at 365.42. In terms of the relative performance of average annual prices, the percentage gains achieved last year were as follows: 

There was an exceptionally strong rebound in demand across all metals in 2010.  The most notably feature was the surge in offtake in the mature economies, which exceeded that of China for the first time in a number of years!  The data on crude steel production, which given its myriad of end uses is a reasonable proxy for industrial commodity demand, reinforces this point.  Chinese crude output increased by 10.1% last year, while output outside of the country increased by 21.6%. 

Chinese base metal consumption growth was held back by destocking; however as we have noted in our earlier reports underlying non-ferrous semis activity and steel output was strong in the country.  For example stainless and galvanized steel output rose by 25% and 60% respectively.  Imports of some base metals into China slipped earlier in the year. However, more recently, they have started to show monthon-month-gains. 

###### Al 30.5; Cu 46.0; Ni 48.4; Pb 24.0; Sn 50.4; Zn 30.1 

Although the percentage increases are obviously also a function of the price performance in 2009 which sets the base, the two top performing metals copper and tin have in our view the best fundamentals.  We expect this to continue to be the case in 2011.  The experience of aluminium and zinc merely confirms the fact that in the current environment, when there is strong investment activity an improvement in the fundamentals is not a “necessary” condition for price increases.  The concept of relative performance of individual metals is becoming increasingly important.  This is one of the reasons we could see further advances for aluminium despite the stock overhang. 

In terms of Chinese production, the market focused on the reduction in supply to power-intensive users such as the base metals sector as part of an attempt to fulfill energy commitments in the most recent Five Year plan.  There are also broader measures to curb small-scale inefficient smelting and refining capacity.  However, analysis of the latest monthly production data shows that these measures have been primarily focused on aluminium with production in November 16% below the peak for the year seen in the summer.  For lead, for example, production in November was at an all-time high, while zinc output was just below the October peak.  Chinese raw material production – alumina and concentrate output increased sharply in 2010, up to 41% and 22% respectively in the case of lead and zinc.  This enabled the gains in refined production despite lower imports of raw materials. 

Many of the broader drivers of the market last year were positive – weak dollar, investment fund activity, China, accelerating global

economic growth, relatively low downstream inventories and continuing supply shortfalls. We will consider which factors will continue to support the market in 2011 below. Although our latest supply-demand projections are similar to those released in December, GFMS have amended our price projections for 2011. With the exception of tin, this has involved an increase to our projections (see individual sections for our price forecasts). For the mature economies, base metal demand will not benefit from the one-off restocking rebound seen in 2010. Base Metals & Other Commodity Prices

On a more positive note for base metal producers downstream inventories are fairly tight, also the anecdotal evidence that we receive suggest that demand is holding up well at present. Nevertheless after the sharp recovery seen in 2010, we are not building further significant advances into our supply demand balance calculations. Although we have noted on numerous occasions that it is difficult to double guess the funds, many of the factors that attracted to the base metal sector are still in place. Base metals as an asset class continue to gain acceptance. This year the market will benefit from the launch of various ETFs. While success of these instruments is yet to become clear, some tonnages will be removed from the market. The base metal sector is increasingly being seen as part of the diversification of asset allocation. In line with a number of other markets, particularly equities, investor interest remains high in a low interest rate environment especially when the bulk of the economic data remains positive. We have seen the downside potential during 2010 during periods of risk aversion, when the sovereign debt problems and some concerns over Chinese growth helped to trigger a massive fall in the base metal markets. GFMS’ Base Metals index fell from 316.44 on April 26 to a low for the year of 231.84 on June 8. There is obviously the potential for a repeat of this with the debt issue in Europe not resolved, but merely shifted to other countries within the region. The latest ISM manufacturing index in the **United States** rose from November’s 56.6 to 57.0. This marks the second increase in the past three months and puts the index at its highest since May. A particularly encouraging sign going forward was the 4.3 point increase to the new orders component of the index to 60.9. Overall, the latest index is consistent with manufacturing activity on an upward trend in early 2011. 

For **Europe** , our favoured indicator is the euro zone economic sentiment index. This increased to 106.2 in December from 105.1 in November and is at its highest level in over 3 years.  Better activity in Germany (see below) was a key driver. Going forward the region will have to cope with the negative impact of fiscal tighten

ing and still high unemployment. Nevertheless growth in the region has consistently surprised to the upside, albeit from a low base. Manufacturing orders in Germany increased by 5.2% monthon-month on a seasonally adjusted basis in November. The strong performance was supported by a sharp rise in exports. Domestic orders also grew in December but at a much slower pace than external demand. Consumption and business spending are being boosted by rising confidence and growth, which has been stronger than expected. Underlying trends in German manufacturing remain encouraging for the coming months. The manufacturing PMI remains well above the neutral level of 50 and reached a five-month high in December. Consumer sentiment improved in December according to the University of Michigan. Its index rose to 74.5, up from 71.6 in November. While the recent gains in confidence are welcome, there are still questionmarks overhanging the consumer sector notably the weak job environment and higher energy prices. The US auto industry finished 2010 on a high with sales at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate of 12.55 million units. Inevitably discounting has played its role. The peak followed a strong performance throughout the month of December, on the back of expectations for ongoing growth in consumption coupled with persistent concerns for supply tightness fuelling investment demand for the metal.
